newsitem.title: USA: Japan says U.S. estimate of trade gap too large.
newsitem.headline: Japan says U.S. estimate of trade gap too large.

text.p: A U.S. estimate that Japan's trade surplus with the rest of the world will expand to $130 billion in 1998 is too large, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official said on Friday.

The official said U.S. President Bill Clinton introduced the estimate when he met with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Thursday ahead of the three-day Group of Seven indstrial countries summit that begins later Friday.
"Japan told U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that the U.S. estimate was too large," the official said. Rubin met Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka earlier on Friday.

During the Rubin-Mitsuzuka meeting, Japan referred to an estimate of the International Monetary Fund that Japan's trade surplus will likely rise to $90 billion. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development forecast $98.4 billion worth of Japan's trade surplus in 1998, the Japanese official said.
Japan's trade surplus stood at 3.55 trillion yen ($31 billion) in 1996, according to Japanese official statistics.
Rubin was quoted by the Japanese official as saying that people will know whose predictions are correct when real data come out.
Japan's trade surplus in May jumped more than 200 percent after more than doubling in April.
The official said the increases in Japan's surplus in April and May were due to temporary factors such as an exceptional rise in auto exports.

Japan's carmakers did not have enough stocks of cars in February and March that can be used for exports as domestic car demand increased sharply in those months ahead of a April 1 rise in Japan's consumption tax to five percent from three percent. This boosted car exports in April and May.
